title: AFK Agents
lesson_subtitle: AFK Agents: Let Your Product Build Itself

tactic.name: Stay Out The Loop
tactic.one_liner: Stop sitting at your device prompting back and forth — build AFK agents (prompt input, trigger, environment, review) so that entire classes of chores, bugs, and features become pull requests while you are away from the keyboard.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: It asks you to let error-prone agents ship real work end-to-end with nobody watching. Dan pre-empts the objection head-on: you might be thinking about how error-prone LLMs and agents can be, or how AI can't possibly ship your special-snowflake work end to end — 'If you are not wrong now, you will be. It's only a matter of time. Tools will change and models will improve.' It also demands upfront investment in a net-new agentic layer around your codebase — 'this is gonna be different, it's gonna be a little challenging' — before any payoff, and it means admitting that most of your daily engineering never required your expertise at all.

mission: Step out of the loop and let your product build itself. Replace and outperform cloud-based agentic coding tools — Copilot, Devin, Jules, Codex — with your own agentic pipeline that knows YOUR codebase, YOUR engineering practices, and YOUR domain-specific problems. Those tools are designed for everyone's codebases, not yours; 'just like the prompt, your agentic pipeline is too valuable to outsource to a third party tool, especially this early in phase two of the generative AI age.' By halfway through TAC you automate the plan and build steps of the software development lifecycle — from prompt to PR — and keep ownership of every piece.

loop_model.in_loop: Human-in-the-loop agentic coding — what most engineers do right now. You sit at your device prompting back and forth, back and forth, burning your time on work that could be handed off. Dan's verdict: great for experimentation, exploring new territory, and very hard, very specific problems — 'but let's be real, most of engineering is not that.' The tech ecosystem is obsessed with it and misses the trend: increasingly more chores, bugs, and features don't require your expertise at all.
loop_model.out_loop: Outloop agentic coding is off-device agentic coding. You write high- to low-level prompts, pass them to your agentic pipeline, and go AFK — away from keyboard. 'You walk away from your keyboard, or maybe you were never there in the first place. Maybe you sent the prompt right from your phone on GitHub, Slack, Notion, Jira, a text message, or any third-party tool.' Because models improve and tools change, every improvement raises what your out-loop system can solve — so you invest in scaling what agents can do instead of doing work yourself.

piter.mnemonic: PITER — Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review (pronounced 'Peter'). The four elements of AFK agents; with this setup, your agents can run while you're AFK.
piter.prompt_input: Where work is stated. Lesson choice: GitHub issues — the issue title and description ARE the prompt the agent executes on. Chores need only a couple of lines (issue #31: '/chore — we need to document the adw/ directory'); features get a high-to-mid-level prompt with constraints (issue #33: JSONL support with 'std lib only', delimiter, and UI requirements).
piter.trigger: What starts the run. Lesson choices: a GitHub webhook (adws/trigger_webhook.py — FastAPI POST /gh-webhook, fires on issues:opened or an issue comment that is exactly 'adw', launches the workflow as a background process to beat GitHub's 10-second webhook timeout), a polling cron (adws/trigger_cron.py — checks every 20 seconds), or a manual command (uv run adw_plan_build.py <issue-number>).
piter.environment: Where the agent runs with full control. Lesson choice for demo 1: a dedicated Mac mini ('IndyDevDanAgents's Mac mini') exposed to GitHub via a Cloudflare tunnel; for demo 2: Dan's local machine with a manual trigger. Dan: the dedicated environment is why running with permissions skipped is acceptable — 'it is running dangerously, but because it's in its own environment, this is going to be safe.'
piter.review: How you inspect finished work. Lesson choice: GitHub pull requests — the ADW pushes a branch and opens a PR with a summary, a link to the committed plan file, 'Closes #<issue>', and the ADW tracking ID. Supporting live feed: every step posts an issue comment ({adw_id}_{agent}: ✅ message).
piter.tool_agnostic: Dan is explicit that the four elements can be anything — GitHub issues or Jira tasks or Notion boards; webhook or cron or manual; Mac mini or any sandbox; PRs or another review surface. 'Don't read into how this is configured too much. Focus on the composable units.' Recommended great defaults: GitHub issues for prompt input, GitHub PRs for review, start the trigger and environment locally, then offload to another device.

adw.definition: An ADW (AI Developer Workflow) is a reusable agentic workflow that combines code, agentic prompts, and agents to deliver results autonomously. It is the highest leverage point and the highest composition level of agentic coding — the synthesis of previous-generation deterministic code and new-generation non-deterministic language models, prompt chains, and now agents.
adw.future_claim: 'In the future these will just be known as scripts and we'll fully expect agentic behavior by default. We're creating a concrete term for this' — the term is pulled forward from Principled AI Coding (Dan's prior course) to be absolutely clear about how powerful and differentiated this unit of engineering is.
adw.anatomy_in_lesson: adws/adw_plan_build.py automates plan + build: (1) fetch GitHub issue, (2) classify it (/chore | /bug | /feature via the issue_classifier agent), (3) create a branch (branch_generator), (4) plan agent (sdlc_planner) runs the matching template to write a specs/*.md plan, (5) plan_finder extracts the plan path, (6) committer commits the plan, (7) build agent (sdlc_implementor) runs /implement on the plan file with a fresh context window, (8) committer commits the implementation, (9) pr_creator opens the PR. Between every step: post an issue comment or fail loudly (check_error exits and reports ❌ to the issue).
adw.many_names: Agentic workflow, agentic pipeline, compositional workflow, ADW — 'so many names for the same thing.' The agentic layer = .claude/commands/ (your prompts) + adws/ (your workflows) wrapped around an untouched app/.

core_concepts.name: Two types of agentic coding: in-loop vs out-loop
core_concepts.plain_english: In-loop: you stay at the device, prompting back and forth — fine for experiments and genuinely hard problems, but it caps how much work you can hand off. Out-loop: off-device — the prompt goes in from anywhere, the pipeline does the work, and a PR comes back. One of them 'lets you hand off exponentially more work to your agents.'
core_concepts.dan_words: "Outloop agentic coding is off-device agentic coding. It's when you write high to low-level prompts that you pass off to your agentic pipeline, then you go AFK, away from keyboard... or maybe you were never there in the first place."
core_concepts.misconception: That out-loop replaces in-loop. Dan keeps both: in-loop is great for experimentation, new territory, and very hard specific problems — the tactic is about recognizing that most engineering is NOT that, and routing the rest out of the loop.

core_concepts.name: Tactic #4: Stay Out The Loop
core_concepts.plain_english: The fourth compressed mental framework of TAC. After stop coding (1), adopt your agent's perspective (2), and template your engineering (3), you now stop babysitting runs entirely: define the work, fire it into your pipeline, and review the PR that comes back. The tactic exploits the one reliable trend — models improve, tools change — so your out-loop system solves more problems every month without you changing anything.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Stay out the loop is a tactic of agentic coding that reinforces the fact that models will improve and tools will change... enabling you to focus on scaling up what your agents can do instead of wasting time doing the work yourself. You build the system that builds the system."
core_concepts.misconception: That staying out of the loop means zero oversight. The R in PITER is load-bearing: 'we'll always need to review' — the loop you leave is the prompting loop, not the review loop. (Lesson 5 then attacks review velocity.)

core_concepts.name: AFK agents
core_concepts.plain_english: Agents that run while you're away from keyboard — 'the agents you'll build to run the loop while you stay out of it.' They live in their own environment, wake on a trigger, execute your templates, and report back through your review system. This is the lesson's answer to cloud coding agents: same convenience, but running YOUR prompts on YOUR codebase.
core_concepts.dan_words: "In order to build Outloop systems, we need AFK agents, agents that run while we're away from the keyboard."
core_concepts.misconception: That AFK agents are a product you buy. The whole point is that they're four composable elements you assemble around your codebase — the lesson's Mac mini + webhook + issues + PRs is one configuration, not the definition.

core_concepts.name: PITER — the four elements of AFK agents
core_concepts.plain_english: Prompt input (where work is stated — GitHub issues here), Trigger (what starts the run — webhook, cron, or manual command), Environment (where the agent runs with full control — a dedicated Mac mini here), Review (how you inspect the result — pull requests here). Remove any one and the system stops being AFK: no input means nothing to do, no trigger means someone must press go, no environment means it runs where you work, no review means you can't trust what shipped.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The four elements are prompt input, the trigger, you'll need an environment, and then a review system. These four elements can be remembered with Peter... With this setup, your agents can run while you're AFK."
core_concepts.misconception: Fixating on the tools instead of the elements. Dan: 'It doesn't matter if you use GitHub issues, if you like Jira tasks, Notion boards, whatever you wanna use. The key is that these four elements are always there.'

core_concepts.name: The ADW — AI Developer Workflow
core_concepts.plain_english: The unit that runs between trigger and review: deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents. In tac-4 it's a single uv single-file Python script (adws/adw_plan_build.py) that chains micro-agents — classifier, branch generator, planner, plan finder, committers, implementor, PR creator — each fired through Claude Code with one slash-command template and one job.
core_concepts.dan_words: "An ADW is a reusable agentic workflow that combines code, agentic prompts, and agents to deliver results autonomously. On the battleground of agentic engineering, the ADW is how you create this new agentic layer around your codebase."
core_concepts.misconception: That the ADW is 'just a script that calls the API.' The composition is the point: templates from lesson 3 become the building blocks, code handles sequencing/errors/reporting, and agents handle judgment — 'the synthesis of previous generation deterministic code and new generation non-deterministic language models.'

core_concepts.name: The agentic layer (two essential directories)
core_concepts.plain_english: The out-loop machinery lives OUTSIDE your application code: .claude/commands/ holds the reusable prompts, adws/ holds the workflows that chain them. app/ is completely untouched — 'we're not combining or conflating the functionality between these two.' That separation is what makes the layer portable to any codebase you operate in.
core_concepts.dan_words: "By dedicating and focusing really hard on these two essential directories — .claude/commands, aka wherever your prompts are stored, and ADWs, [where] compositional workflows are stored — you wanna create this outer layer to automate the different classes of software engineering problems that you have."
core_concepts.misconception: Mixing the layer into the app (importing app code from ADWs or vice versa). The lesson's directory discipline — app/ untouched by adws/ — is a design rule, not an accident of the demo.

core_concepts.name: The issue IS the prompt
core_concepts.plain_english: The prompt input element turns your tracker into an agent interface: the issue title + body become the prompt. A chore needs two lines; a feature gets a 'high to mid-level prompt' with constraints (std-lib only, __ delimiter in a constants file, _0 list indexing, update the UI, create test fixtures). You focus on the what; the how is already encoded in your templates.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We'll create new issues, and the title and description will be the prompt that our agent will execute on... We're focusing on the what, not the how. The details of how things are done, we've already encoded into our codebase via our reusable prompts, our templates and our meta prompts."
core_concepts.misconception: Writing the plan into the issue. The planner exists precisely so you don't: 'All I have to do is write the prompt, the high level prompt, not even the plan.' Weak students either over-specify (doing the planner's job) or under-specify (no constraints, then blame the agent).

core_concepts.name: Micro-agents: isolate the big three per step
core_concepts.plain_english: Each ADW step is its own agent with its own fresh context window, its own prompt template, and its own model choice. The classifier only classifies; the planner only plans; the implementor starts clean with the plan as its prompt. This is why the pipeline stays reliable across many steps — and why you can put a cheap fast model on classification and your most powerful model on plan and build.
core_concepts.dan_words: "By separating our agents, we're able to isolate the big three — context, model, prompt — to solve one problem and solve one problem well... Its context window is completely free. We can select a more powerful model, which I recommend you do for the implementation."
core_concepts.misconception: One mega-agent with one giant prompt doing classify+plan+build in a single run. The lesson's architecture argues the opposite: small, specialized, observable steps — the same reason a lot of agentic tools fail is they don't understand your codebase OR your decomposition.

core_concepts.name: Claude Code in programmable mode as the composable primitive
core_concepts.plain_english: Every agent in the ADW is one subprocess call: claude -p '<slash_command> <args>' --model <model> --output-format stream-json --verbose --dangerously-skip-permissions. The tac-1 seed ('the agent is a function') is now industrialized: agent.py builds the command, saves the prompt, streams JSONL to agents/{adw_id}/{agent}/raw_output.jsonl, and parses the result message for success, session_id, and output.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is the value of programmable mode. This is why it's so powerful. It lets us use Claude Code as a new agentic coding primitive, where we can call our agent with any prompt at any step of our workflow that we need to automate engineering work."
core_concepts.misconception: That --dangerously-skip-permissions is reckless. In an interactive session it would be; here it's paired with the E of PITER — 'it is running dangerously, but because it's in its own environment, this is going to be safe.' The permission model moved from the tool to the environment boundary.

core_concepts.name: Structured return contracts between agents and code
core_concepts.plain_english: Deterministic code can only chain non-deterministic agents if outputs are machine-checkable. Every glue template ends with a contract: classify_issue → 'Respond exclusively with /chore, /bug, /feature, or 0'; generate_branch_name → 'Return ONLY the branch name'; commit → 'Return ONLY the commit message'; pull_request → 'Return ONLY the PR URL'; find_plan_file → 'the path or 0'. The Python validates and fails loudly on anything else.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We have a nice mapping here. Of course, if you have more detailed or different classes of problems, you just add them here in your classify issue step, and then you update your data types to support the different types of slash commands that you solve."
core_concepts.misconception: Letting agents reply in prose and parsing vibes. The '0 if not found' escape hatch matters as much as the happy path — code needs a deterministic failure signal, not an apology paragraph.

core_concepts.name: Observability: report, log, monitor
core_concepts.plain_english: Three layers make the AFK run legible: (1) live feed — every step posts an issue comment prefixed {adw_id}_{agent_name}; (2) per-run artifacts — agents/{adw_id}/{agent}/ holds the exact prompt sent and the full raw_output.jsonl (plus a readable .json); (3) per-session logs — Claude Code hooks write logs/{session_id}/*.json for every tool call. The plan itself is committed as a spec file, so you can read exactly what the implementor was told to do.
core_concepts.dan_words: "It doesn't matter if our agent can solve every problem if we don't know that it's solved. We need to observe, we need to report, we need to log and monitor."
core_concepts.misconception: Treating logging as optional plumbing to add later. In an out-loop system observability IS the product: without the live feed and artifacts you can't review, and without review you can't improve templates — the improvement loop dies.

core_concepts.name: Solve problem classes; fix the system, not the issue
core_concepts.plain_english: ADWs + templates solve classes of problems — chores, bugs, features — not individual tickets. So when a run gets something wrong (the chore PR mislabeled ADW as 'Agentic Developer Workflow'), you don't hand-patch the output; you improve the prompt/template that produced it, and every future run inherits the fix.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Every time you miss something, what do you do? You don't fix the issue. You fix the system that caused the issue. You fix your templates, you fix your ADW."
core_concepts.misconception: Grading the system on one imperfect PR and quitting. Dan on camera finds errors in his own demo PR and narrates the correct response: 'this is something that I need to improve in my prompt to be clearer.' You won't start with top-tier KPIs — you run, invest in templates, compose, improve.

core_concepts.name: The trust ladder: chores → bugs → features
core_concepts.plain_english: Adoption path for the tactic: start with chores ('the simplest unit of engineering work that your agent should be taking off your plate with no debate at all'), graduate to bugs, then full features. Each rung builds trust in your ADW and improves your templates before the stakes rise.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Start with low hanging fruit, build up trust in your ADW and your system... Start templating out the chore for your codebase, then move up to bugs, and then eventually you'll get to the feature level."
core_concepts.misconception: Starting with your gnarliest feature to 'really test it,' watching it fail, and concluding out-loop doesn't work. The ladder exists because the KPIs start mediocre by design — trust is built, not assumed.

core_concepts.name: Why this improves the agentic KPIs
core_concepts.plain_english: Lesson 2's four KPIs return as the scoreboard: presence (human-in-the-loop interactions) down, size (operations completed by agents) up, streak (successful one-attempt prompts in a row) up, attempts (prompts before task completion) down. Staying out of the loop is presented as the single best lever on all four at once.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This directly ties into our ability to improve our agentic coding KPIs. We want presence down, size up, streak up, and attempts down. What's the best way to accomplish great agentic coding KPIs? You guessed it, stay out the loop and focus on building the system that builds the system."
core_concepts.misconception: Reading the KPIs as vanity metrics. They're the review rubric for your ADW runs: a run that needed you three times scored presence=3, and the fix is template/system work, not more prompting.

core_concepts.name: Own your pipeline (vs cloud agentic tools)
core_concepts.plain_english: Copilot, Devin, Jules, Codex are great — Dan has used them all — but they're 'literally designed for everyone's codebases, not yours.' They don't run your templates, your prompts, or your engineering standards, so they plateau exactly where your product becomes unique and differentiated. The DIY four-element stack costs one setup afternoon and compounds with every template improvement.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Yes, it's true. There are cloud-based tools that do this workflow, but that's not exactly true. These tools are not running your templates. They're not running your prompts. They're not built to solve your problems... this one size does not fit all, especially as your product grows and becomes unique and differentiated."
core_concepts.misconception: Hearing this as 'never use cloud tools.' The claim is narrower and sharper: the pipeline — the encoding of how YOUR team ships — is too valuable to outsource, especially this early in phase two; rent compute if you like, but own the pipeline.

programmable_mode.why_it_matters: tac-1 proved the agent is a callable function (claude -p). tac-4 builds a production-shaped system on that primitive: agent.py wraps the call with model selection, stream-json output captured to per-agent JSONL files, prompt archiving, result-message parsing (success flag + session_id + final text), and an environment allowlist so the subprocess sees only the variables it needs (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CLAUDE_CODE_PATH, PATH/HOME/USER/SHELL/TERM, optional GITHUB_PAT exported as GH_TOKEN, optional E2B_API_KEY). This is the mechanism that lets ONE Python file orchestrate eight specialized agent invocations per feature.
programmable_mode.invocation: cmd = [CLAUDE_PATH, "-p", prompt, "--model", model, "--output-format", "stream-json", "--verbose"] + ["--dangerously-skip-permissions"] (execute_template always enables it); prompt = f"{slash_command} {' '.join(args)}" — slash commands resolve to .claude/commands/*.md templates with $ARGUMENTS / $1 $2 $3 substitution.

step_by_step_demo: (8:30–8:56) The four elements named: prompt input, trigger, environment, review — remembered with PITER; this lesson runs two ADWs automating the plan and build steps of the SDLC.

(9:09–10:29) Element choices for demo 1: GitHub issues as prompt input (title + description = the prompt); a GitHub webhook as trigger (configured, URL blurred on camera); a dedicated Mac mini as environment (screen-shared, `uv run adws/trigger_webhook.py` waiting on port 8001); GitHub PRs as review.

(10:29–11:11) Demo 1 prompt input: new issue 'ADW Documentation' → body: '/chore — we need to document the adw/ directory. Read everything in adw/ then update README.md with information about how it works.' Chores are the simplest unit of engineering work — hand them off with no debate.

(11:11–12:09) Issue created (#31) → webhook fires → the Mac mini boots the workflow. The issue comments become a live feed: '5615f7c8_ops: ✅ Starting ADW workflow' → '✅ Issue classified as: /chore' → '✅ Working on branch: chore-31-5615f7c8-document-adw-directory' → '5615f7c8_sdlc_planner: ✅ Building implementation plan'.

(12:09–13:03) Micro-agent architecture narrated while it runs: classifier, branch generator, planner — each isolates the big three to solve one problem well. Planner commits its spec file; the implementor then starts with a completely free context window (and could use a more powerful model — recommended for implementation).

(13:28–14:20) Implementation committed, PR created — all on the agent's own device. 'Here comes the PR. There it is. ADW completed.' Total time for the chore: about five minutes. The high-level prompt was expanded into a plan (exactly the lesson-3 pattern), then built.

(14:34–15:56) Review the PR (#32, 'chore: #31 - ADW Documentation'): clean top-to-bottom write-up — summary, implementation plan link (specs/adw-documentation-plan.md), changes made, files changed (README.md + the plan), ADW tracking ID 5615f7c8, 'Closes #31'. Dan spots real errors to encode away: the PR expands ADW as 'Agentic Developer Workflow' — 'that's just wrong. This is something that I need to improve in my prompt to be clearer.'
(16:38–17:42) Recap of PITER for demo 1, then demo 2 setup: kill the webhook listener (trigger off), switch environment to the local device and trigger to a manual script run.

(17:55–20:17) Fresh clone flow: git clone tac-4, open IDE, boot Claude Code ('I'm gonna run in Yolo mode because I understand everything this codebase will and can do — if you're ever worried about the permissions, always check the settings file'), then /install: reads .env.samples (never .env), primes on the codebase, removes the course remote + git init, cp .env.sample .env, installs FE/BE deps, tries ./scripts/copy_dot_env.sh (tac-2 may not exist — proceeds either way), then REPORTS work completed + action required — including pushing to your OWN new GitHub repo so you have your own issues and PRs.

(20:17–21:08) Root .env: the two keys that matter are ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ('the agent SDK currently only runs with the API key — this may change in the future') and CLAUDE_CODE_PATH (run `which claude` and paste the value if plain 'claude' fails).

(21:08–22:57) Demo 2 prompt input: boot the app (sh scripts/start.sh — backend :8000, frontend :5173), tour the NL→SQL interface (upload CSV/JSON, query 'users age descending' → SQL against local SQLite), note uploads accept only .csv/.json today, then write issue #33 'Jsonl Support': add JSONL upload; scan the whole file for fields; std lib only; one table per file like CSV/JSON; concat nested fields with __ stored as an updatable delimiter in a constants file; _0 indexing for lists; update the UI; create test .jsonl fixtures in the test dir.

(22:57–24:31) Health check first — 'something I highly recommend you build into your ADWs before you run your complex or simplistic workflow': uv run adws/health_check.py 33 → env vars OK, git repo OK (with the built-in warning if your remote still points to disler — update it so you get YOUR issues and PRs), GitHub CLI installed+authenticated, Claude Code live-test passed (2+2 → 4), health comment posted to issue #33. Good to go.

(24:31–25:39) Manual trigger: copy the usage line from adw_plan_build.py, drop the optional adw-id, run `uv run adw_plan_build.py 33` — note it must be run as adws/adw_plan_build.py (Dan's first attempt errors with 'Failed to spawn'). ADW ID cb881e79 assigned; issue classified /feature; branch feat-33-cb881e79-jsonl-support created; 'our agent has taken the wheel. We are now out of the loop.'

(26:05–26:59) The live feed shows '✅ Issue classified as: /feature' — the classify step routes to a completely different meta-prompt template than the chore. 'We can target specific classes of problems with this switch.'

(26:59–31:51) Code walkthrough while the feature builds: the workflow docstring at the top of adw_plan_build.py (fetch issue → branch → plan agent → build agent → PR); main() = parse args, make ADW ID, set up logger, check env, get repo from git remote, fetch typed issue (Pydantic GitHubIssue); the report-or-check-error pattern between every step; classify_issue as an isolated slash-command prompt ('no ad hoc prompts as strings inside of the codebase — everything's isolated so that we can improve it'); the data_types Literal mapping you extend for new problem classes; build_plan showing the AgentTemplateRequest shape (agent_name, slash_command, args, model) — Sonnet used on camera for speed, top models recommended for plan and build.

(31:51–32:43) agent.py execute step: build the prompt, save it, run Claude Code in programmable mode — the full command with --output-format stream-json and --dangerously-skip-permissions, safe because of the dedicated environment. 'It lets us use Claude Code as a new agentic coding primitive.'

(32:43–34:28) Observability tour: per-session log files (logs/{session_id}/, activated via Claude Code hooks); per-ADW agent folders — agents/cb881e79/ shows adw_plan_build (execution log), branch_generator, issue_classifier, plan_finder, sdlc_planner, sdlc_planner_committer, sdlc_implementor, sdlc_implementor_committer, pr_creator; each holds the saved prompt and raw_output.jsonl (+ pretty .json).

(34:28–35:47) Feature workflow completes: PR #34 in ~17 minutes end-to-end. Review: key features handled, comprehensive test coverage, front-end updated, sample fixtures created — and the committed 170-line plan ('the planner created the plan and outputted a concrete asset... this lets you improve — it's not enough to just run a random ad hoc prompt because how will you know how to improve that? And more importantly, how will your agents know?').

(35:47–38:28) Verify like an engineer: boot client+server on the feature branch, regression-test an existing query (users descending — unchanged), confirm the upload UI now says CSV, JSON or JSONL, drag-drop the agent-created sample_data.jsonl fixture → table lands with the __ concatenation and _0 list indexing exactly as specified. 'This feature was created in one shot... This was a feature that an engineer may have picked up themselves, and it was completely unnecessary.'

(38:41–39:49) Infra notes: the webhook is exposed via a Cloudflare tunnel (cloudflared) — use anything; the key is a dedicated environment so a GitHub issue created anywhere kicks off your workflows no matter where they run.

(43:11–44:30) Adoption plan: take action now — 'the ROI here is insane'; start with a simple chore end-to-end to hit the aha moment; great defaults are GitHub issues + PRs; run trigger/environment locally first, then offload to another device; climb chores → bugs → features.

quotes.text: In this lesson, you step out of the loop and you let your product build itself.

By the end of this lesson, you'll know exactly how to replace and outperform modern cloud-based agentic coding tools like Copilot, Devin, Jules, Codex... they lack the detail needed to ship end-to-end in your codebase, with your engineering practices, for your domain-specific problem.
Just like the prompt, your agentic pipeline is too valuable to outsource to a third party tool, especially this early in phase two of the generative AI age.

The tech ecosystem has become obsessed with human in the loop systems and most fail to recognize the trend that there are increasingly more chores, bugs, and features that don't require your expertise at all.

GitHub CLI (gh) installed and authenticated — the ADW's entire GitHub surface runs through it
A GitHub repo YOU own (push the cloned course code to a new remote so you have your own issues and PRs; /install walks you through it)

what_student_must_internalize: Two types of agentic coding exist — in-loop and out-loop — and out-loop ('off-device') is what lets you hand off exponentially more work. In-loop survives for experimentation, new territory, and genuinely hard problems; most engineering is not that.

AFK agents = four composable elements, PITER: Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review. The elements are invariant; the tools (issues/Jira, webhook/cron/manual, Mac mini/anything, PRs) are yours to choose.

An ADW is deterministic code orchestrating non-deterministic agents through reusable prompt templates — 'code, agentic prompts, and agents' delivering results autonomously. Lesson 3's templates are the building blocks; the ADW is the composition.
The agentic layer is architecturally separate: .claude/commands/ + adws/ wrap an untouched app/. That separation is what makes the layer reusable across codebases.

Micro-agent decomposition is the reliability trick: each step isolates the big three, gets a fresh context window, its own template, and its own model (cheap+fast for glue steps, most powerful for plan and build).

Code↔agent handoffs need structured return contracts ('Respond exclusively with...', 'Return ONLY...', '0 if not found') plus loud failure (comment ❌ on the issue and exit). No ad hoc prompt strings in the codebase — every prompt is an isolated, improvable file.

Observability is load-bearing: issue-comment live feed with {adw_id}_{agent} prefixes, per-run agents/{adw_id}/ artifacts (saved prompts + raw JSONL), per-session hook logs, and the committed plan file. 'It doesn't matter if our agent can solve every problem if we don't know that it's solved.'
The plan is a committed artifact precisely so you (and your agents) know how to improve — the anti-'random ad hoc prompt' principle.
When output is wrong, fix the system that caused it (template/ADW), never just the artifact. ADWs solve problem classes, not tickets.
Adoption is a trust ladder — chores, then bugs, then features — and the payoff is measured in the lesson-2 KPIs: presence down, size up, streak up, attempts down.
Owning your pipeline beats renting one: cloud agentic tools can't run your templates or your standards, and one size does not fit all as your product differentiates.
Dangerous flags become safe through environment isolation, not through hope — the permission boundary moves from the tool to the dedicated environment.

Writing the plan into the issue (or a one-word issue with zero constraints). The issue is a high-to-mid-level prompt: what + constraints. The planner fills in the how.
Watching the live feed like a movie but never opening agents/{adw_id}/ or the committed plan — then having no idea what to fix when a run goes sideways.

teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) the difference between in-loop and out-loop agentic coding, and which classes of work belong in each; (2) the four PITER elements and the concrete tool Dan chose for each in the lesson — then re-map all four onto YOUR team's stack; (3) how adw_plan_build.py chains micro-agents (classifier → branch → planner → plan-finder → committer → implementor → committer → PR) and why each gets a fresh context window and an isolated prompt template; (4) why every glue prompt ends with 'Return ONLY...' and what the code does when that contract breaks; and (5) what Dan did when his own demo PR contained an error — and why 'fix the system, not the issue' is the sentence that makes the whole tactic compound.

retrieval_questions.q: What are the two types of agentic coding, and what is out-loop in one phrase?
retrieval_questions.a: In-loop (human in the loop, prompting back and forth at the device) and out-loop — off-device agentic coding: pass high-to-low-level prompts to your pipeline and go AFK.

retrieval_questions.q: Expand PITER and name the lesson's tool choice for each element.
retrieval_questions.a: Prompt input (GitHub issues — title+description are the prompt), Trigger (GitHub webhook; also shown: cron polling and a manual command), Environment (a dedicated Mac mini the agent fully controls; demo 2 uses the local device), Review (GitHub pull requests, plus the issue-comment live feed).

retrieval_questions.q: Define an ADW in Dan's words and name the two directories that form the agentic layer.
retrieval_questions.a: A reusable agentic workflow that combines code, agentic prompts, and agents to deliver results autonomously. The layer = .claude/commands/ (reusable prompts) + adws/ (the workflows), wrapped around an untouched app/.

retrieval_questions.q: List the micro-agents adw_plan_build.py fires, in order, for a feature issue.
retrieval_questions.a: issue_classifier (/classify_issue), branch_generator (/generate_branch_name), sdlc_planner (/feature — or /chore, /bug per classification), plan_finder (/find_plan_file), sdlc_planner_committer (/commit), sdlc_implementor (/implement <plan>), sdlc_implementor_committer (/commit), pr_creator (/pull_request).

retrieval_questions.q: What exact classification outputs does the classifier contract allow?
retrieval_questions.a: /chore, /bug, /feature — or 0 if none apply; anything else fails validation and the run reports the error to the issue and exits.

retrieval_questions.q: How does the webhook trigger beat GitHub's 10-second timeout, and what two events start a run?
retrieval_questions.a: It responds immediately and launches adw_plan_build.py as a background process (subprocess.Popen). Triggering events: an issue being opened, or a new issue comment whose body is exactly 'adw'.

retrieval_questions.q: Where do you look to understand a finished (or failed) AFK run? Name all the observability layers.
retrieval_questions.a: The issue-comment live feed ({adw_id}_{agent}: ✅/❌ message), agents/{adw_id}/<agent>/ (saved prompt + raw_output.jsonl + .json + execution.log), logs/{session_id}/ from Claude Code hooks, the committed specs/*.md plan, and the PR body with the ADW tracking ID.

retrieval_questions.q: Why is --dangerously-skip-permissions acceptable in this system?
retrieval_questions.a: Because the agent runs in its own dedicated environment (the E of PITER): 'it is running dangerously, but because it's in its own environment, this is going to be safe.' The permission boundary is the environment, not the tool dialog.

retrieval_questions.q: What model advice does Dan give for ADW steps?
retrieval_questions.a: He runs Sonnet on camera for speed, but recommends throwing your most powerful models at the most complex steps — the plan and the build/implement steps.

retrieval_questions.q: Your ADW's PR describes ADW as 'Agentic Developer Workflow' (wrong). What is the correct response, per the lesson?
retrieval_questions.a: Don't just fix the PR text — fix the system that caused it: improve the prompt/template (and data types if needed) so every future run is correct. 'You don't fix the issue, you fix the system that caused the issue.'

retrieval_questions.q: What is the recommended adoption path and the four KPIs this tactic moves?
retrieval_questions.a: Start with chores, then bugs, then features (build trust in the ADW). KPIs: presence down, size up, streak up, attempts down.

retrieval_questions.q: How long did the two demo runs take end-to-end, and what came back for review each time?
retrieval_questions.a: The documentation chore: about 5 minutes (issue #31 → PR #32). The JSONL feature: about 17 minutes (issue #33 → PR #34, including a 170-line committed plan and test fixtures) — verified live by uploading a .jsonl file the agent created.

retrieval_questions.q: Why does Dan say cloud agentic coding tools have 'natural limits' for your work?
retrieval_questions.a: They're designed for everyone's codebases, not yours — they don't run your templates, your prompts, or your engineering practices, and one size does not fit all as your product becomes unique and differentiated. Own your pipeline instead.

retrieval_questions.q: What must be true of every glue-step prompt's output, and why?
retrieval_questions.a: It must satisfy a machine-checkable contract ('Return ONLY the branch name / commit message / PR URL / path — or 0'), because deterministic code chains the steps and needs to validate or fail loudly, commenting ❌ on the issue and exiting.

AgentTemplateRequest(agent_name, slash_command, args, adw_id, model='sonnet') and AgentPromptRequest(model default 'opus', dangerously_skip_permissions, output_file) — models are Literal['sonnet','opus']. ClaudeCodeResultMessage documents the stream-json result line (num_turns, duration_ms, total_cost_usd, session_id...). current_practice_gaps.gap: Hand-rolled subprocess wrapper → Claude Agent SDK
current_practice_gaps.why: agent.py's subprocess + stream-json parsing + env allowlist is exactly what the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) now provides as a supported surface: typed message streams, structured outputs, session management, hooks, subagents, permission control. Dan even flags the aging edge on camera: 'the agent SDK currently only runs with the API key — this may change in the future.' The lesson's teaching form (see every moving part) remains the best way to LEARN the primitive; production builds today should reach for the SDK.

current_practice_gaps.gap: DIY issue→PR pipelines now have first-party competitors (and hosts)
current_practice_gaps.why: Since recording, GitHub-native coding agents (Copilot coding agent assignable to issues, Claude Code GitHub Actions with @claude mentions) productized the issue→PR loop, and CI runners became a mainstream Environment choice for the E in PITER. Dan's core argument is strengthened, not weakened: those tools still don't run YOUR templates/standards — but a modern reader should know the four elements can be hosted on GitHub Actions instead of a Mac mini, and that 'replace the cloud tools' now includes 'or bring your pipeline INTO their infrastructure.'

The lesson's stance (dangerous flag + dedicated environment = safe) predates current options: sandboxed bash, permission modes, --allowedTools/--disallowedTools for headless runs, hook-based gates, and container/worktree isolation. The PRINCIPLE (move the boundary to the environment) is unchanged and correct; the mechanism menu is richer, and teams now often prefer scoped allowlists over full skip even inside sandboxes.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Reusable prompts as .claude/commands → Agent Skills / richer command surfaces
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson's prompt library is flat .md slash commands with $1/$2/$ARGUMENTS. Current Claude Code adds Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter, on-demand loading, composability) and richer slash-command features — the modern packaging for the same 'no ad hoc prompts, isolate to improve' doctrine. Concept transfers 1:1; the book should teach commands first (visible mechanics), then show the Skills upgrade path.

health_check.py hardcodes claude-3-5-haiku-20241022 for its live test; the ADW passes 'sonnet'/'opus' aliases from a course-era model family. Aliases still resolve, but the families have moved (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era). Treat specific IDs as period detail; the transferable advice is the model-per-step policy — cheapest model that solves the glue step, most powerful on plan/build.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Single serial ADW → fleets, queues, and parallel isolation
current_practice_gaps.why: adw_plan_build runs one issue at a time in one working copy; concurrent webhook fires would collide in the same checkout (branch switching mid-run). Current practice runs ADWs in parallel via git worktrees, containers, or queued runners, with concurrency guards. The course intentionally scales this in later lessons ('we're gonna push this a lot further') — flag the ceiling so nobody productionizes the demo as-is.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Issue-comment live feed → structured run dashboards
current_practice_gaps.why: Comments-as-telemetry is still a great zero-infra pattern, but current stacks add structured run views (GitHub Actions job summaries, Checks API, OpenTelemetry-style traces of agent steps) on top. The lesson's deeper rule — observe/report/log/monitor or you can't improve — is timeless.

setup: Clone the course repo: git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-4.git && cd tac-4

Create a warm-up issue on YOUR repo, then run the pre-flight: cd into the repo and run `uv run adws/health_check.py <issue-number>` — required outcome: HEALTHY, no 'disler' warning, and a ✅ comment on your issue

Read everything in adw/ then update README.md with information about how it works.' Run `uv run adws/adw_plan_build.py <A>` (root-run 'Failed to spawn' is the expected first stumble). Watch the issue comments drain: Starting → classified /chore → branch → planner → plan file → commits → PR.

Verify the chore run like a grader: branch name matches <class>-<issue>-<adw_id>-<slug>; specs/*-plan.md committed on the branch; two commits in the '<agent>: <class>: <message>' format; PR body has plan link + 'Closes #A' + ADW ID. Then AUDIT the PR content against the real code (the demo PR mislabeled 'AI Developer Workflow' and described files that don't exist) — write down every inaccuracy you find and WHICH template would prevent it (chore.md? pull_request.md?).

FEATURE RUN: create issue B titled 'Jsonl Support' with Dan's constraints verbatim (std lib only; scan whole file for fields; one table per .jsonl like csv/json; concat nested fields with __ via an updatable delimiter in a constants file; _0 for list items; update the UI; add .jsonl test fixtures under app/server/tests). Run `uv run adws/health_check.py <B>`, then `uv run adws/adw_plan_build.py <B>`. Expect roughly 15–20 minutes.

While it runs, open a second terminal and trace the run live: tail agents/<adw_id>/adw_plan_build/execution.log; after each step, inspect agents/<adw_id>/<agent>/prompts/*.txt and raw_output.json — connect every issue comment to the artifact that produced it.

Review the feature PR: read the committed plan first, then files changed, then run the validation the plan claims: git checkout the feature branch, cd app/server && uv run pytest (green), sh scripts/start.sh, regression-test an old query, and drag-drop the agent-created .jsonl fixture — confirm the __ and _0 conventions in the resulting table. Merge only if YOU would merge it.

TRIGGER DRILLS: (a) cron — run `uv run adws/trigger_cron.py`, comment exactly 'adw' on issue A, watch it re-process within ~20 seconds, then Ctrl+C; (b) webhook — run `uv run adws/trigger_webhook.py`, expose it (scripts/expose_webhook.sh with a Cloudflare tunnel token, or ngrok), configure a GitHub webhook for Issues + Issue comments to <url>/gh-webhook, create a tiny chore issue from your PHONE, and watch a PR appear. (Optional if you can't provision a tunnel — say so explicitly rather than skipping silently.)
Reset utilities between runs: scripts/clear_issue_comments.sh <n> and scripts/delete_pr.sh <n> [--delete-branch]; stop everything with scripts/stop_apps.sh and scripts/kill_trigger_webhook.sh.
